name: Trimipramine
summary: Sedating tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) sometimes used for depression with prominent insomnia or agitation. Can work well for mood, but the side effect burden is real (anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, cardiac risk), and it is generally avoided in older adults.
description: Trimipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant that can help depression—especially when sleep is wrecked and you need a more sedating option. It usually takes 1–2 weeks to notice early changes and 4–6 weeks for fuller benefit. This medication can cause strong sedation, constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, and low blood pressure when standing. It can also affect heart rhythm, so it’s not a casual prescription. Like other antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning about increased suicidal thoughts/behaviors in people 24 and younger, especially early on or with dose changes.
patient_summary: Trimipramine is a sedating antidepressant sometimes chosen when depression comes with major insomnia or nighttime anxiety. It can help mood over weeks, but it can also cause heavy drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, and blood-pressure drops when you stand up. It can affect heart rhythm and is usually avoided in people 65+. If you’re 24 or younger, antidepressants can raise suicidal thinking early in treatment—so you need close check-ins, especially during the first month and after dose changes.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Tricyclic Antidepressant (Tertiary Amine), Highly Sedating and Anticholinergic

linked_conditions.context: Used to treat depression. Clinically, it’s most relevant when depression is paired with significant insomnia, agitation, or nighttime anxiety because it is strongly sedating.

Not a primary insomnia medication, but its strong sedation can be useful when insomnia is a major part of the depressive picture. This is a side-effect-driven benefit, not a first-line insomnia strategy.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to trimipramine, any component of the formulation, or other tricyclic antidepressants
Use during the acute recovery phase of myocardial infarction
Concurrent use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or use within 14 days of discontinuing either trimipramine or an MAOI
Initiation of trimipramine in a patient receiving IV methylene blue

efficacy_response.metric: Time to clinically meaningful improvement in depression
efficacy_response.patient_text: With trimipramine, early improvement can show up in 1–2 weeks, but the full antidepressant effect usually takes 4–6 weeks. If nothing is moving by week 4 at an adequate dose, your clinician will usually reassess the plan.

pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: initial effects may be observed within 1 to 2 weeks; continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be taken without regard to food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Trimipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant used to treat depression. In real-world psych practice, the main reason it ever comes up is when depression is tangled up with bad insomnia, nighttime anxiety, or agitation and you need a more sedating antidepressant. It’s not a first-pick medication for most people because the side effect and safety profile can be rough compared with newer options.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Depression, especially when sleep is severely disrupted or anxiety is worse at night
Depression with prominent agitation or restlessness where a sedating antidepressant is clinically helpful
off_label: Insomnia in the context of depression (sedation-driven, not first-line)
Nighttime anxiety as part of a depressive episode (as part of the overall depression treatment plan)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s different, but trimipramine tends to create a pretty consistent “feel” because it’s so sedating and anticholinergic:

quotes: It didn’t just help me sleep—it basically switched me off.
I slept, but I woke up feeling like I got hit by a drowsy truck.
My brain was calm at night for the first time in months… but mornings were rough.
items.note: Sedation is common and can be intense, especially at the beginning or after dose increases.

quotes: The sleep improved first. Mood followed later—more like weeks than days.
By week two I felt less hopeless, but it wasn’t dramatic overnight.
It was subtle: fewer spirals, less crying, more “I can handle today.”
items.note: Antidepressant benefit usually builds over weeks, not hours.

items.category: Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision (classic TCA stuff)
quotes: My mouth was so dry I carried water everywhere.
Constipation was the surprise side effect nobody warned me about.
My vision felt weird and blurry, especially at night.
items.note: These are anticholinergic effects and can become a deal-breaker for some people.

quotes: If I stood up fast, I saw stars.
I had to move slower—especially in the morning.
It helped my mood, but I felt unsteady sometimes.
items.note: Orthostatic hypotension (blood pressure dropping when you stand) is a known issue with this medication.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Trimipramine can make you sleepy early, but the antidepressant effect takes time.
key_points: First dose to first effects: Sedation can show up quickly (often the first night)
1–2 weeks: Early antidepressant changes may start (energy, sleep rhythm, fewer intrusive negative thoughts)
4–6 weeks: Typical window for fuller antidepressant benefit
1–6 hours: Peak blood levels after a dose

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.value: Early improvement often within 1–2 weeks; fuller response commonly 4–6 weeks
sections.text: Trimipramine is an antidepressant option that can work for depression, but it’s typically chosen for a specific clinical fit—when sedation is actually helpful (severe insomnia, nighttime anxiety, agitation). If you tolerate it, the sleep benefit may show up before mood improves, and the mood benefit usually builds over several weeks.
sections.clinical_details: Clinically, trimipramine is generally not a first-line antidepressant because the side effect burden (sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostasis) and cardiac safety considerations can outweigh the benefits for many patients. When used, clinicians often focus on careful dosing, bedtime administration when possible, and close monitoring early in treatment.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warning: Antidepressants can increase suicidal thinking/behavior in children, teens, and young adults (18–24), especially early in treatment and with dose changes.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior (suicidality) in short-term studies in children, adolescents, and young adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Closely observe patients of all ages who are started on therapy for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior—especially during the first 1 to 2 months and during dose increases or decreases. Trimipramine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
other: Overdose danger: TCAs have a narrow safety margin in overdose. If suicide risk is high, clinicians typically prescribe the smallest reasonable quantity.
Cardiac risk: Can affect conduction and rhythm. Use extra caution with existing heart disease or history of arrhythmias.
Severe sedation: Can impair driving, reaction time, and decision-making—especially when starting or after dose changes.
Anticholinergic burden: Constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion are not minor side effects with this medication.
Orthostatic hypotension: Can cause dizziness and falls, especially when standing quickly or if you’re dehydrated.
Mania/hypomania risk: Can flip bipolar depression into hypomania/mania. Screen for bipolar disorder before antidepressant monotherapy.
Serotonin syndrome: Possible when combined with other serotonergic medications; monitor for agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, and fever.
patient_counseling: If you’re 24 or younger: treat the first month like a “high monitoring” period. Any sudden mood worsening, agitation, or suicidal thoughts = contact your clinician immediately.
Tell someone you trust you’re starting the medication. A second set of eyes matters.
Avoid driving or risky tasks until you know how sedating it is for you.
Hydrate and stand up slowly—especially in the morning.
Constipation and urinary retention are common. Don’t just “power through” it—tell your prescriber early.
If you have a history of bipolar symptoms (periods of decreased sleep + increased energy + impulsive behavior), say that out loud before starting.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Trimipramine is one of the more sedating, more anticholinergic antidepressants. The side effects tend to be predictable: heavy drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, dizziness, and sometimes heart-related effects.
plain_language_list: Urinary retention (trouble peeing) in susceptible people
Sexual side effects (changes in libido, erectile issues)

common.incidence: Frequency not defined in product labeling
common.patient_note: This can be strong. Many people take it at bedtime for that reason. The goal is “sleepy enough to sleep” without being a zombie the next morning.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision)
common.incidence: Frequency not defined in product labeling
common.patient_note: These effects can stack up. Constipation can become severe if you ignore it. If you get urinary retention or eye pain/vision halos (glaucoma warning sign), that’s urgent.

common.incidence: Frequency not defined in product labeling
common.patient_note: Standing up quickly can make you lightheaded. This is a fall risk. Hydration and slow position changes matter.

common.incidence: Frequency not defined in product labeling
common.patient_note: Some people feel foggy or slowed down—especially early on or at higher doses.

common.incidence: Frequency not defined in product labeling
common.patient_note: Yes, it’s paradoxical sometimes: you can be sedated and still have fragmented sleep or vivid dreams.

serious: Cardiac arrhythmias, conduction problems, tachycardia, and (rarely) myocardial infarction or stroke symptoms—seek emergency care for chest pain, fainting, severe palpitations, or neurologic symptoms.
Seizures (risk increases with higher doses, predisposition, or interacting meds).
Severe confusion, hallucinations, or worsening psychosis in vulnerable patients.
Serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic agents: agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, diarrhea—medical emergency.
SIADH / hyponatremia (low sodium), especially in older adults: confusion, weakness, headache, falls.
Agranulocytosis or significant blood count issues (rare): fever, sore throat, infections—urgent evaluation.
Cholestatic jaundice or significant liver enzyme elevation (rare): yellow skin/eyes, dark urine—urgent evaluation.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Trimipramine has meaningful interaction risk—especially with MAOIs, other serotonergic meds, and anything that worsens sedation, blood pressure drops, or heart rhythm risk.

items.with: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and IV methylene blue
items.risk: Contraindicated due to risk of serious reactions (including serotonin toxicity).
items.action: Wait 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting trimipramine, and also 14 days between stopping trimipramine and starting an MAOI.

items.with: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, buspirone, St. John’s wort, tryptophan)
items.action: Avoid risky combinations when possible; if used, monitor closely for agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, fever, and neuromuscular changes.

items.with: Alcohol, benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds, muscle relaxants
items.risk: Additive CNS depression: heavier sedation, impaired coordination, accidents, falls.
items.action: Minimize or avoid combining sedatives. If unavoidable, use the lowest effective doses and avoid driving.

items.with: Medications that increase arrhythmia/QT risk or worsen conduction
items.risk: Higher risk of rhythm problems and conduction abnormalities.
items.action: Clinicians may check ECG and electrolytes in higher-risk patients and avoid stacking QT/conduction-risk meds.

items.risk: May inhibit metabolism of some TCAs and increase toxicity risk.
items.action: Avoid or use cautiously; monitor for increased sedation, dizziness, or other toxicity.

items.risk: Manufacturer labeling lists it as contraindicated, but some newer evidence suggests serotonin syndrome risk may be low; risk may increase with longer concurrent use.
items.action: If the combination is medically necessary, clinicians monitor closely for serotonin toxicity and educate on symptoms.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on trimipramine for more than a few weeks, don’t stop abruptly. Tapering helps prevent discontinuation symptoms and helps your clinician see whether symptoms returning are withdrawal vs depression coming back.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: A common approach is tapering over 2–4 weeks.
If treatment lasted 2–3 weeks: Often taper over 1–2 weeks.
<2 weeks of treatment: Many people don’t need a taper, but clinical judgment matters.
Go slower (≥4 weeks) if you’ve had withdrawal symptoms before or you’re on higher doses.
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: Return to the prior dose and taper more gradually.
Some patients on long-term antidepressants (>6 months) and/or with a history of discontinuation syndrome may need a very slow taper (sometimes >3 months).
Discontinuation symptoms can include nausea, dizziness, sweating, tremor, sleep disruption/vivid dreams, anxiety, irritability, mood swings, and—less commonly—heart rhythm symptoms with TCAs.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Trimipramine is typically started low and increased gradually. Many clinicians prefer moving the dose toward bedtime once tolerated because sedation is a major effect. Dosing varies depending on outpatient vs inpatient setting, tolerability, and comorbid medical risk.

adult.depression_initial: 25 to 50 mg/day PO at bedtime or in divided doses (some hospitalized patients may start at 100 mg/day)
adult.depression_titration: Gradually increase based on response and tolerability
adult.maintenance: Lowest effective dose, typically given as a single bedtime dose once stable
adult.administration_notes: May take with or without food. Initial dosing may be divided; maintenance dosing is commonly consolidated to bedtime due to sedation.

sections.simple_explanation: This is an older-style antidepressant where dose increases are usually gradual. People often feel sedation early, but mood improvement takes weeks. Because it can cause dizziness and heart-related issues, clinicians are careful with dose changes—especially in higher-risk patients.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Trimipramine is not a first-line antidepressant for many special populations because of side effects and safety considerations, but it may be continued in select cases when it’s been effective and alternatives are riskier. Decisions are individualized and ideally shared between patient and clinician.
sections.pregnancy: Pregnancy exposure data for tricyclic antidepressants (including trimipramine) exist but are limited and mixed. Untreated depression also carries real risks in pregnancy (including relapse, functional impairment, and adverse pregnancy outcomes). If a patient is stable on trimipramine before pregnancy, some may continue it after a risk–benefit discussion. During pregnancy and postpartum, therapeutic drug monitoring can be considered because drug levels may shift. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible and monitor symptoms with a validated tool.
sections.lactation: It is not known if trimipramine is present in breast milk. If used while breastfeeding, infants should be monitored for sedation and poor feeding. If initiating a brand-new antidepressant during breastfeeding, many clinicians prefer agents with more lactation data, but continuation of an effective TCA may be considered depending on clinical need and individual risk–benefit discussion.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for pediatric use. Antidepressants carry increased suicidality risk in children, adolescents, and young adults. Also, controlled trials have not consistently shown TCAs to be superior to placebo for pediatric depression, and safer contemporary options are generally preferred. If used in adolescents in rare cases, reduced dosing and close monitoring are standard.
sections.geriatrics: Generally avoid in adults 65+ because trimipramine is highly anticholinergic and highly sedating, and it increases risk of orthostatic hypotension and falls. If it must be used, clinicians typically start with a low dose (up to 50 mg/day) and titrate cautiously, with a typical maximum around 100 mg/day in older adults and close monitoring for confusion, constipation/urinary retention, and blood pressure drops.
sections.hepatic: No manufacturer-provided adjustment, but use caution because it’s hepatically metabolized. Some experts recommend starting and maintaining at ~50% lower doses in hepatic impairment with cautious titration based on response and tolerability.
sections.renal: eGFR ≥15 mL/minute: No adjustment typically required. eGFR <15 mL/minute or dialysis: Use a low initial dose up to 50 mg/day and increase gradually based on response and tolerability.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidal ideation and clinical worsening: Baseline and closely during the first 1–2 months and with dose changes (increases or decreases).
Sedation and functional impairment: Daytime drowsiness, driving safety, reaction time, work/school functioning—especially early on.
Orthostatic blood pressure and falls: Check standing/sitting blood pressure and ask about dizziness and near-falls.
Cardiac monitoring: ECG, heart rate, and blood pressure in patients with cardiac disease or higher arrhythmia/QT risk; monitor for palpitations, syncope, chest pain.
Electrolytes: Potassium, magnesium, and sodium at baseline and as clinically indicated (especially sodium in older adults due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk).
Liver function tests: Baseline and as clinically indicated.
Weight and BMI: Baseline and periodically.
Blood glucose: Baseline and as clinically indicated in patients with diabetes or glucose regulation concerns.
Bipolar screening and mood switches: Watch for hypomania/mania (decreased sleep, increased energy, impulsivity, irritability).
Discontinuation symptoms when tapering: Dizziness, nausea, sweating, tremor, sleep disruption, mood lability; adjust taper speed if symptoms flare.
If therapeutic drug monitoring is used: Draw trough level just before the next dose; typical therapeutic range cited as 150 to 300 ng/mL; alert level 600 ng/mL.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Trimipramine is available as oral capsules/tablets depending on the country. Clinicians often aim for bedtime dosing once stabilized because sedation is prominent.
items: United States (generic): Oral capsules 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg
Canada (generic): Oral tablets 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Trimipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant. Its antidepressant effect is thought to involve changes in serotonin signaling over time, with downstream “resetting” of mood circuits rather than an immediate switch-flip effect. Clinically, what you feel right away is often sedation—not antidepressant action.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Trimipramine is not a modern first-line antidepressant for most patients. Where it can make sense is a narrower lane: depression with severe insomnia or nighttime agitation where sedation is a feature, not a bug. Even then, clinicians weigh the tradeoffs—anticholinergic side effects, blood pressure drops, and cardiac considerations. In older adults, it’s generally avoided. In patients with meaningful suicide risk, prescribers are often extra cautious because TCAs are more dangerous in overdose than many newer antidepressants.

seo.title: Trimipramine: Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, Warnings & Tapering
seo.description: Trimipramine is a sedating tricyclic antidepressant used for depression—often when insomnia is severe. Learn dosing, side effects (dry mouth, constipation, dizziness), suicidality warning in young adults, interactions, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Trimipramine is used to treat depression. In psychiatry, it’s most relevant when depression comes with severe insomnia, nighttime anxiety, or agitation—because this medication is strongly sedating.

faqs.q: How long does trimipramine take to work for depression?
faqs.a: Sedation can happen quickly (sometimes the first night), but that’s not the same thing as antidepressant benefit. Early mood changes may show up in 1–2 weeks, and fuller improvement often takes 4–6 weeks.

It can help sleep because it’s very sedating, but it’s not usually prescribed as a pure insomnia medication. It’s more of a “depression treatment where sleep is a major symptom” option—because the side effect profile can be heavy.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones are sleepiness (sometimes intense), dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, dizziness when standing, and feeling foggy or slowed down. These are classic tricyclic/anticholinergic effects.

faqs.q: Why do clinicians avoid trimipramine in older adults?
faqs.a: Because it’s highly anticholinergic and highly sedating, and it can cause orthostatic hypotension. In people 65+, that combination raises the risk of confusion, constipation/urinary retention, falls, and fractures—so it’s generally avoided.

faqs.q: Does trimipramine have a suicidality warning?
faqs.a: Yes. Like other antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning that suicidal thinking and behavior can increase in children, adolescents, and young adults (18–24) during short-term studies—especially early in treatment and during dose changes. Close monitoring is essential.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on trimipramine?
faqs.a: It’s a bad idea. Alcohol can stack on top of trimipramine’s sedation and make you more impaired, more unsteady, and more likely to have accidents or falls. If you drink, talk to your prescriber about what’s safe for you—many people are advised to avoid it.

faqs.q: What medications should not be combined with trimipramine?
faqs.a: MAO inhibitors are the big hard stop—you need a 14-day washout in either direction. Also be cautious with other serotonergic meds (serotonin syndrome risk) and other sedatives (excess sedation and falls). Your clinician will review your full med list for heart-rhythm risk stacking too.

faqs.q: How do I taper off trimipramine?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or more, many clinicians taper over 2–4 weeks to reduce discontinuation symptoms and to watch for relapse. If you get significant withdrawal symptoms, the usual move is to go back to the previous dose and taper more slowly.

faqs.q: Is trimipramine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It depends on the individual situation. There’s some pregnancy outcome data for TCAs, but it’s limited and mixed, and untreated depression also carries real risks. Breast milk data for trimipramine specifically are unclear. If someone is stable on it, continuation may be considered after shared decision-making, with close monitoring.
